quiz: Think about what sits directly beneath the hypervisor: the bare hardware, or a full general-purpose host OS.
A VM has two layers of addresses. Think about how hardware can do both translations without the hypervisor faking tables.
Most guest instructions run at native speed. Think about which kinds the hypervisor must step in and handle itself.
Each namespace isolates one kind of thing. Match the one that gives a process its own numbering tree.
The name says what it isolates: user and group ids. Why would a different id inside versus outside matter for safety?
memory.max is a hard limit. When reclaim fails, the kernel must free memory inside that group somehow.
cpu.max is a quota of CPU time per period. Think about what happens once the quota is used up early.
Lower layers are never changed, and a file must be fully present somewhere writable before a write can land. What must happen first?
You cannot delete from a read-only lower layer. The upper layer must hide the file with a special marker.
Ask how much work each call does when only a handful of 100K connections have data. Does it depend on all fds or only active ones?
Edge-triggered mode reports only changes. Think about what happens if you leave unread data behind.
epoll tells you when you may act; io_uring works differently. Think about where requests and results live and how often you enter the kernel.
Count copies between page cache, user buffer and socket buffer, and the user/kernel switches for two syscalls.
Encryption must happen somewhere on the data path. Think about where a user-space TLS library runs and why that matters.

Confirm with exit code and cgroup events, separate container-level from node-level OOM, then fix leaks or adjust limits.
Explain the CPU quota per period shared by all threads, how bursts hit throttling, and how to see and fix it.
Describe merging read-only lower layers with a writable upper layer, lookup order, copy-up on first write, and whiteouts.
Compare the limits, how interest sets are passed each call, and whether cost grows with all descriptors or only ready ones.
Explain level versus edge triggering, when each fits, and the rule to use non-blocking descriptors and drain until EAGAIN.
Contrast readiness with completion, explain the shared submission and completion rings, and fewer syscalls and file I/O support.
Count CPU copies, DMA copies and context switches for both paths, and explain how sendfile skips the user buffer.
Explain that encryption must touch every byte, so plain zero-copy breaks, and cover options like kernel TLS and NIC offload.
Define both types with examples, then explain how KVM turns Linux into a hypervisor and why it is debated which type it is.
Start from the threat model, then layer defences: micro-VMs or sandboxes, least privilege, network limits and resource limits.
Cover event loops per core with epoll, small per-connection memory, file descriptor limits, kernel buffer and port tuning.
